<!-- The interactive isogeny graph. Used on the home page and on the Animations pages
     through Quarto's include shortcode (see index.qmd), followed by a <script type="module"> tag loading assets/js/isogeny-hero.js (the path
     is relative to the page). To start in the growing-ball animation instead of the
     random walk, wrap the include in  ::: {data-mode="ball"}  ...  :::
     The data (assets/data/isogeny/) is made by _scripts/isogeny_graphs.py. -->

```{=html}
<figure class="wm-graph" id="wm-graph">
  <!-- THE INFO PANEL. One block per entry of the animation menu (data-anim is the entry's
       value). The script shows the block of the animation that is running, so the title,
       description and parameters always belong to what is on screen. To change what is
       said about an animation, edit its block here. -->
  <div class="wm-anim-info">
    <section data-anim="view" data-title="Graph viewer" hidden>
      <p class="wm-anim-title">Graph viewer</p>
      <p>The graph, with nothing moving. A vertex is a supersingular elliptic curve up to isomorphism over the algebraic closure of F<sub>p</sub>, labelled by its j-invariant; an edge is an ℓ-isogeny. Where the numbers of isogenies in the two directions differ, each one is drawn with an arrowhead; this happens next to a vertex with automorphisms other than ±1, and everywhere in the Γ<sub>1</sub>(5) graph. Hover or tap a vertex for its label, and drag to rearrange.</p>
      <p class="wm-anim-params"><span>Parameters</span> graph · view · p · j labels</p>
    </section>
    <section data-anim="walk" data-title="Random walks" hidden>
      <p class="wm-anim-title">Random walk</p>
      <p>A walker starts at a random vertex and moves along the edges. The laser is the step being taken and the trail is its recent history. <span class="wm-anim-which">This is the simple random walk: at each step every isogeny out of the current vertex is equally likely, and an arrow is followed only forwards.</span> The walk is switched off when the graph shown is not connected.</p>
      <p class="wm-anim-pi" aria-live="polite"></p>
      <p class="wm-anim-params"><span>Parameters</span> graph · view · p · history (how many recent steps stay highlighted) · speed</p>
    </section>
    <section data-anim="cycle" data-title="Blooming for collision" hidden>
      <p class="wm-anim-title">Blooming for collision</p>
      <p>A ball grows around a vertex one layer at a time (breadth-first search) and stops when it runs into itself: an edge reaches a vertex already in the ball, other than along the edge it came in by. That closes a cycle, shown in bold. A loop counts as a cycle of length 1, and two parallel edges as one of length 2. Tap a vertex to start from it.</p>
      <p class="wm-anim-params"><span>Parameters</span> graph · view · p · speed</p>
    </section>
    <section data-anim="ball" data-title="Blooming for conjugates" hidden>
      <p class="wm-anim-title">Blooming for conjugates</p>
      <p>A ball grows around a vertex one layer at a time and stops when it contains a vertex w together with its Frobenius conjugate w<sup>(p)</sup> ≠ w. Where it stopped is red, and the shortest paths from the centre are bold. In the quotient by Frobenius it stops when it reaches a vertex a second time by the other lift, or reaches a vertex fixed by Frobenius. Tap a vertex to start from it.</p>
      <p class="wm-anim-params"><span>Parameters</span> graph · view (full graph or quotient by Frobenius) · p · speed</p>
    </section>
    <section data-anim="spectral" data-title="Spectral law" hidden>
      <p class="wm-anim-title">Spectral law (Kesten–McKay)</p>
      <p>For a prime ℓ ≠ p, the eigenvalues of the Hecke operator T<sub>ℓ</sub> on the weight-2 cusp forms S<sub>2</sub>(Γ<sub>0</sub>(p)) are the eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix of G<sub>p</sub>(ℓ) other than ℓ + 1. The histogram shows them for about 100 primes p from 101 to 20011, against the Kesten–McKay density (red). The corner shows the Kolmogorov distance between the two. Serre proved that they agree in the limit p → ∞.</p>
      <p class="wm-anim-params"><span>Parameters</span> ℓ · speed</p>
    </section>
  </div>
  <div class="wm-graph-controls">
    <div class="wm-graph-kinds">
    <div class="wm-seg" role="group" aria-label="Which isogeny graph to draw">
      <button type="button" data-kind="2" aria-pressed="true">ℓ = 2</button>
      <button type="button" data-kind="23" aria-pressed="false">2, 3</button>
      <button type="button" data-kind="235" aria-pressed="false">2, 3, 5</button>
      <button type="button" data-kind="2b5" aria-pressed="false">2 · Γ₀(5)</button>
      <button type="button" data-kind="23b5" aria-pressed="false">2, 3 · Γ₀(5)</button>
      <button type="button" data-kind="2g15" aria-pressed="false">2 · Γ₁(5)</button>
      <button type="button" data-kind="3g2" aria-pressed="false">3 · Γ(2)</button>
      <button type="button" data-kind="3g4" aria-pressed="false">3 · Γ(4)</button>
      <button type="button" data-kind="5g4" aria-pressed="false">5 · Γ(4)</button>
    </div>
    <button type="button" class="wm-q" data-terms="supersingular isogeny graph2 level loops directed" aria-label="What are these graphs?" aria-expanded="false">?</button>
    </div>
    <div class="wm-graph-selects">
      <label class="wm-graph-view">view
        <select aria-label="Full graph, F_p-subgraph, or quotient by Frobenius">
          <option value="full" selected>full graph</option>
          <option value="spine">𝔽ₚ-subgraph</option>
          <option value="folded">quotient by Frobenius</option>
          <option value="over" hidden>over the 𝔽ₚ-subgraph (level structure)</option>
        </select>
      </label>
      <button type="button" class="wm-q" data-terms="full spine folded over frobenius pair" aria-label="What do full graph, F_p-subgraph and quotient by Frobenius mean?" aria-expanded="false">?</button>
      <label class="wm-graph-prime">p = <select aria-label="Characteristic p"></select></label>
      <label class="wm-graph-labels"><input type="checkbox" checked> j labels</label>
      <button type="button" class="wm-q" data-terms="p jinv fp" aria-label="What is p?" aria-expanded="false">?</button>
    </div>
  </div>
  <div class="wm-graph-stage">
    <svg class="wm-graph-svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="wm-graph-caption"></svg>
    <a class="wm-graph-eye" href="/animations/about.html" data-base="/animations/about.html" data-tip="Learn more about this graph" aria-label="Learn more about this graph">
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" width="20" height="20" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M1.5 12S5.5 4.5 12 4.5 22.5 12 22.5 12 18.5 19.5 12 19.5 1.5 12 1.5 12Z" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" stroke-linejoin="round"/><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="3.4" fill="currentColor"/></svg>
    </a>
    <div class="wm-graph-tip" hidden></div>
  </div>
  <div class="wm-graph-walk">
    <label class="wm-graph-walk-label">animation
      <select class="wm-graph-anim" aria-label="Which animation to run">
        <option value="view" selected>graph viewer</option>
        <option value="walk">random walk</option>
        <option value="cycle">blooming for collision</option>
        <option value="ball">blooming for conjugates</option>
        <option value="spectral">spectral law (Kesten–McKay)</option>
      </select>
    </label>
    <label class="wm-graph-ell">ℓ =
      <select aria-label="Which Hecke operator T_ℓ">
        <option value="2" selected>2</option>
        <option value="3">3</option>
        <option value="5">5</option>
      </select>
    </label>
    <button type="button" class="wm-q" data-terms="viewer walk cycle ball spectral km" aria-label="What do the animations show?" aria-expanded="false">?</button>
    <label class="wm-graph-history">history
      <select class="wm-graph-trail-len" aria-label="Number of recent steps to keep highlighted">
        <option value="10" selected>10 steps</option>
        <option value="25">25 steps</option>
        <option value="50">50 steps</option>
        <option value="100">100 steps</option>
        <option value="250">250 steps</option>
      </select>
    </label>
    <button type="button" class="wm-graph-play" aria-label="Pause the animation">Pause</button>
    <label class="wm-graph-speed-label">speed
      <select class="wm-graph-speed" aria-label="Speed of the random walk">
        <option value="calm">calm</option>
        <option value="fast" selected>fast</option>
        <option value="frantic">frantic</option>
      </select>
    </label>
  </div>
  <figcaption>
    <span class="wm-graph-caption" id="wm-graph-caption">Supersingular isogeny graphs: the objects I study.</span>
    <span class="wm-graph-ball-status" aria-live="polite" hidden></span>
    <span class="wm-graph-stats"></span>
    <span class="wm-graph-legend">
      <span><i class="wm-key wm-key-node"></i>supersingular curve</span>
      <span class="wm-graph-legend-pair" hidden><i class="wm-key wm-key-pair"></i>conjugate pair {E, E<sup>(p)</sup>}</span>
      <span class="wm-graph-legend-fp"><i class="wm-key wm-key-fp"></i><span>fixed by Frobenius</span></span>
      <span><i class="wm-key wm-key-2"></i>2-isogeny</span>
      <span class="wm-graph-legend-arrow" hidden><i class="wm-key wm-key-arrow"></i>one isogeny, in the direction of the arrow</span>
      <span class="wm-graph-legend-3" hidden><i class="wm-key wm-key-3"></i>3-isogeny</span>
      <span class="wm-graph-legend-cls" hidden><i class="wm-key wm-key-node"></i><i class="wm-key wm-key-c1"></i>the two Weil-pairing classes</span>
      <span class="wm-graph-legend-frob" hidden><i class="wm-key wm-key-frob"></i>Frobenius</span>
      <span class="wm-graph-legend-5" hidden><i class="wm-key wm-key-5"></i>5-isogeny</span>
      <span class="wm-graph-legend-spec"><i class="wm-key wm-key-bar"></i>eigenvalues (histogram) <i class="wm-key wm-key-3"></i>Kesten–McKay density</span>
      <span class="wm-graph-legend-ball"><i class="wm-key wm-key-ball"></i>ball <i class="wm-key wm-key-hit"></i>shortest paths to the conjugate pair (red)</span>
      <span class="wm-graph-legend-walk"><i class="wm-key wm-key-walk"></i><i class="wm-key wm-key-trail"></i>laser walker; trail of the last <span class="wm-trail-n">10</span> steps</span>
      <button type="button" class="wm-q" data-terms="supersingular fp pair directed lambda" aria-label="What do the colours and numbers mean?" aria-expanded="false">?</button>
    </span>
    <span class="wm-graph-field"></span>
    <span class="wm-graph-hint"><a href="/animations/">More animations →</a></span>
  </figcaption>
  <div class="wm-graph-pop" role="dialog" aria-label="Explanation" hidden></div>
  <details class="wm-graph-glossary">
    <summary>What do these terms mean?</summary>
    <dl>
      <dt data-term="supersingular">Supersingular curve (a vertex)</dt>
      <dd>An elliptic curve in characteristic p with no point of order p, even over the algebraic closure. Up to isomorphism over the algebraic closure there are about p/12 of them, and each has a model defined over F<sub>p²</sub>.</dd>
      <dt data-term="jinv">j-invariant</dt>
      <dd>A number that identifies an elliptic curve up to isomorphism over the algebraic closure of F<sub>p</sub> (over a finite field, two curves with the same j-invariant can be twists that are not isomorphic); it labels the vertices (switch labels off with <em>j labels</em>; on big graphs, hover instead). It lies in F<sub>p²</sub> and is written a + bi, with i as in the note under the graph; a ± bi labels a conjugate pair in the quotient by Frobenius. With level structure the label is j(E).</dd>
      <dt data-term="isogeny">ℓ-isogeny (an edge)</dt>
      <dd>A map between two curves, given by rational functions, that respects the group law and has a kernel of ℓ points. A curve has ℓ + 1 of them, one for each subgroup of order ℓ: three 2-isogenies (blue), four 3-isogenies (red), six 5-isogenies (green).</dd>
      <dt data-term="graph2">ℓ = 2; ℓ = 2, 3; ℓ = 2, 3, 5</dt>
      <dd>The same vertices, joined by the ℓ-isogenies for the ℓ listed: G<sub>p</sub>(2), G<sub>p</sub>({2,3}) and G<sub>p</sub>({2,3,5}).</dd>
      <dt data-term="level">Level structure: Γ<sub>0</sub>(5), Γ<sub>1</sub>(5), Γ(2)</dt>
      <dd>A vertex is a curve E with extra data, which an isogeny φ: E → E′ of degree prime to the level carries along. <strong>Γ<sub>0</sub>(5)</strong>: a subgroup C of order 5, edge (E, C) → (E′, φ(C)); about 6 vertices per curve. <strong>Γ<sub>1</sub>(5)</strong>: a point P of order 5 up to sign, edge (E, ±P) → (E′, ±φ(P)); about 12 vertices per curve. This graph is directed, because the dual isogeny leads back to (E, ±2P). <strong>Γ(2)</strong> (full level 2): an ordered basis (P, Q) of E[2]; these are the Legendre invariants λ, (p − 1)/2 of them. <strong>Γ(4)</strong> (full level 4): an ordered basis of E[4], 4(p − 1) vertices; the Weil pairing e<sub>4</sub>(P, Q) = ±i splits them into two classes, which 3-isogenies swap and 5-isogenies preserve, so "5 · Γ(4)" is disconnected. The label before the · says which isogenies are edges.</dd>
      <dt data-term="loops">Loops and parallel edges</dt>
      <dd>Two curves can be joined by several isogenies, drawn as parallel arcs, and an isogeny from a curve to itself is drawn as a loop.</dd>
      <dt data-term="directed">Arrowheads</dt>
      <dd>Edges are counted by kernels, so the graph is directed: A<sub>ij</sub> is the number of subgroups K of E<sub>i</sub> with E<sub>i</sub>/K ≅ E<sub>j</sub>. For most pairs A<sub>ij</sub> = A<sub>ji</sub>, and each such pair of opposite isogenies is drawn as one plain edge. Next to a vertex with automorphisms other than ±1 (without level structure: j = 0 and j = 1728) the two counts differ. There every isogeny is drawn on its own, with an arrowhead. The Γ<sub>1</sub>(5) graph is directed everywhere.</dd>
      <dt data-term="p">p</dt>
      <dd>The characteristic, a prime: the curves live over finite fields with p<sup>k</sup> elements. The graph has about p/12 vertices, so a larger p gives a larger graph.</dd>
      <dt data-term="fp">Fixed by Frobenius (gold)</dt>
      <dd>A vertex isomorphic to its Frobenius image. Without level structure this means its j-invariant lies in F<sub>p</sub> (b = 0). With level structure Frobenius moves the level structure too, so it is a stronger condition: (E, C) ≅ (E<sup>(p)</sup>, C<sup>(p)</sup>), i.e. the pair is defined over F<sub>p</sub>.</dd>
      <dt data-term="frobenius">Frobenius</dt>
      <dd>Raising every coordinate to the p-th power sends a curve E to a curve E<sup>(p)</sup> and a subgroup K of E to a subgroup K<sup>(p)</sup> of E<sup>(p)</sup>; on j-invariants it is a + bi ↦ a − bi. It sends the edge E → E/K to the edge E<sup>(p)</sup> → E<sup>(p)</sup>/K<sup>(p)</sup>, so it is a symmetry of the whole graph, on vertices and on edges. Applying it twice gives back every vertex and edge, except with Γ<sub>1</sub>(5) structure when p ≡ ±2 (mod 5), where it takes four applications.</dd>
      <dt data-term="pair">Conjugate pair</dt>
      <dd>A vertex E and its Frobenius image E<sup>(p)</sup>, when the two are different.</dd>
      <dt data-term="full">Full graph</dt>
      <dd>Every vertex and every edge.</dd>
      <dt data-term="spine">F<sub>p</sub>-subgraph (the spine)</dt>
      <dd>The subgraph induced on the vertices fixed by Frobenius: those vertices and every edge of the graph between them, whether or not Frobenius fixes the edge. With level structure it can be empty (the "?" in the empty box says why). When it is not connected the random walk is switched off.</dd>
      <dt data-term="over">Over the F<sub>p</sub>-subgraph (level structure only)</dt>
      <dd>An alternative display of the F<sub>p</sub>-part of a graph with level structure: all vertices (E, ·) whose curve has j(E) in F<sub>p</sub>, i.e. the vertices lying over the F<sub>p</sub>-subgraph of the graph without level structure, and the edges between them. The ones fixed by Frobenius (gold) form the F<sub>p</sub>-subgraph proper; dashed lines join each other vertex to its Frobenius image.</dd>
      <dt data-term="folded">Quotient by Frobenius</dt>
      <dd>Its vertices are the orbits of Frobenius on vertices (a conjugate pair becomes one vertex, drawn larger with a gold ring) and its edges are the orbits of Frobenius on edges. Two parallel edges with conjugate kernels between two vertices with j in F<sub>p</sub> are swapped by Frobenius and become one edge.</dd>
      <dt data-term="viewer">Graph viewer</dt>
      <dd>Just the graph: hover or tap a vertex for its label, drag to rearrange. The other entries of the animation menu animate it.</dd>
      <dt data-term="walk">Random walk</dt>
      <dd>The simple random walk on the directed graph shown, starting from a random vertex: at each step the walker takes one of the edges out of its vertex, each with the same probability, and follows arrows only forwards. On G<sub>p</sub>(ℓ) each of the ℓ + 1 kernels is equally likely. The laser beam shows the step being taken; <em>history</em> is how many recent steps stay highlighted; <em>speed</em> is how fast it moves.</dd>
      <dt data-term="cycle">Blooming for collision</dt>
      <dd>A ball grows from a vertex one layer at a time (breadth-first search) until it collides with itself: an edge reaches a vertex already in the ball, closing a cycle (a loop counts as length 1, two parallel edges as length 2). The cycle is shown in bold. Works in every view; tap a vertex to start there.</dd>
      <dt data-term="ball">Blooming for conjugates</dt>
      <dd>The ball of radius r around a vertex v is the set of vertices at most r steps from v. It grows one layer at a time until it contains a conjugate pair {w, w<sup>(p)</sup>} (in the quotient by Frobenius: until it reaches a vertex by a second lift, or reaches the F<sub>p</sub>-subgraph), then shows shortest paths from v. Tap a vertex to start there.</dd>
      <dt data-term="spectral">Spectral law</dt>
      <dd>The eigenvalues of the Hecke operator T<sub>ℓ</sub> on S<sub>2</sub>(Γ<sub>0</sub>(p)), the weight-2 cusp forms of level p, are the eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix of G<sub>p</sub>(ℓ) other than ℓ + 1. The animation shows their histogram for larger and larger p, against the Kesten–McKay density, and the Kolmogorov distance between the two.</dd>
      <dt data-term="km">Kesten–McKay law</dt>
      <dd>The distribution with density (ℓ+1)√(4ℓ − x²) / (2π((ℓ+1)² − x²)) on [−2√ℓ, 2√ℓ]: the spectral measure of the infinite (ℓ+1)-regular tree. Serre proved that the eigenvalues of T<sub>ℓ</sub> on S<sub>2</sub>(Γ<sub>0</sub>(p)) become distributed according to it as p → ∞.</dd>
      <dt data-term="lambda">Second-largest eigenvalue</dt>
      <dd>The largest eigenvalue of the adjacency matrix is the number of edges at each vertex; the next largest in absolute value measures how fast random walks spread out (smaller is faster). For a single ℓ it is at most 2√ℓ, the Ramanujan bound (Pizer, using Deligne's bound), so at most 2√2 for ℓ = 2. With several ℓ the adjacency matrices commute, so it is at most the sum of these bounds: 2√2 + 2√3 for ℓ = 2, 3, and 2√2 + 2√3 + 2√5 for ℓ = 2, 3, 5. That sum is larger than the Ramanujan bound for a graph of the combined degree, so only the graphs with a single ℓ are called Ramanujan here.</dd>
    </dl>
  </details>
</figure>
```
